sharh: The fullest useful starting point is the extended account of al-Miswar ibn Makhramah and Marwān in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Book of Conditions, nos. 2731–2732, compared with the related concise report, nos. 2711–2712, and Ibn Hishām's Sīrah. Suhayl ibn ʿAmr contested the treaty wording, Abū Jandal's arrival tested its return clause, ʿUmar objected to the terms, and Umm Salamah counselled the Prophet to begin the concluding rites.

The extended treaty account in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Book of Conditions, nos. 2731–2732, can be compared with the concise report, nos. 2711–2712, and with Ibn Hishām's Sīrah. Suhayl ibn ʿAmr, Quraysh's negotiator and Abū Jandal's father, disputed the treaty wording as his son's arrival tested the return clause. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, a leading Companion, questioned the terms; Umm Salamah, the Prophet's wife, advised him to begin the concluding rites.

matn: In North Africa and Egypt, al-Mursī and Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh transmitted the teaching of Abū al-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī; Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh connected remembrance and reliance upon God with ordinary work.

In North Africa and Egypt, the Sufi teacher Abū al-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī's guidance was carried by his successor al-Mursī and by the Egyptian writer Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh, who connected remembrance and reliance upon God with ordinary work.
